clinician.trajectory_summary: An 86-year-old man presented with progressive dyspnea, fatigue, and palpitations. Initial workup showed elevated PSA (total 130 ng/mL) and bone scintigraphy suggested probable bone metastases. One month later, he developed pancytopenia (Hb 6.2 g/dL, platelets 51,000/µL, leukocytes 3950/µL) and was referred to an oncologist who prescribed degarelix for metastatic prostate cancer. Fifteen days after degarelix initiation, he presented to the ED with frank dyspnea and pancytopenia, requiring blood transfusion. Further investigation for pancytopenia revealed normal B12/folate, reticulocytosis, and increased LDH. A bone marrow biopsy confirmed diffuse bone marrow replacement by metastatic adenocarcinoma, with PSA stain consistent with prostatic origin. Staging imaging (kidney US, abdomen CT) showed widespread metastases including lymph nodes and pulmonary nodules. He was then started on docetaxel, leuprolide, and zolendronic acid. After four cycles, he showed no significant improvement, and palliative care was initiated, with the patient requiring two hemotransfusions.
